system_message:
You are generating a synthetic but clinically grounded
conversation for exactly one hospital admission.

Rules:
1. Use only facts supported by the provided admission context.
2. The discharge notes are the backbone of the hospital-course
   narrative. Use them first.
3. The ordered problem list should shape the main clinical focus.
4. Radiology, procedures, microbiology, and the previous-admission
   summary are supporting context, not a checklist.
5. Not every packet item needs to appear in the conversation.
6. Speakers must be exactly: Doctor and Patient.
7. Every conversation line must contain:
   - turn number
   - exact timestamp
   - speaker
   - text
8. Timestamps must be monotonically increasing and stay within the
   admission start and admission end times.
9. Keep the conversation medically plausible and understandable to
   a patient.
10. Use short natural exchanges, patient questions, clarifications,
    explanations, reassurance, and follow-up discussion.
11. Do not invent unsupported diagnoses, procedures, test findings,
    or outcomes.
12. Do not mention the dataset, packet, note types, or that the
    conversation is synthetic.
13. Generate the conversation first, then write the summary strictly from the generated conversation_lines.
14. Every claim in summary.summary_paragraph and every item in summary.problems must be explicitly supported by the conversation_lines.
15. Return output that exactly matches the required JSON schema.
task_message:
Generate one rich patient-doctor conversation for this admission and one admission summary.

Generation guidance:
- Approximate stay length: 4 day(s).
- Recommended turn range: 50-70 turns.
- Exact admission window: 2169-04-03 04:06:00 to 2169-04-06 15:55:00.
- Focus first on the discharge-note storyline and the core admission problems.
- Use radiology, procedures, and microbiology only as supporting detail when they help the story.
- Do not try to mention every packet item.
- Let the conversation unfold across admission, mid-course updates, and discharge planning.
- Prefer many short natural exchanges over a few long summary turns.
- The patient should ask questions, express concerns, seek clarification, and respond to updates throughout the stay.
- The doctor should explain results, treatment changes, progress, and follow-up in multiple conversational beats over time.
- You may paraphrase and add natural conversational glue, but do not invent unsupported diagnoses, procedures, findings, or outcomes.
- Generate the conversation first, then derive the final summary only from the conversation_lines you wrote.
- The final summary must contain admission start time, admission end time, one paragraph summary, and a list of problems.
- Final self-check before returning JSON: turn_number contiguous from 1; conversation_lines.time nondecreasing and inside the exact admission window; summary.admission_start and summary.admission_end copied exactly from the packet; no conversation line has empty text.

previous_admission_summary_used.summary_paragraph: The patient was admitted for laparoscopic Roux-en-Y gastric bypass due to class III morbid obesity with a BMI of 40. She also had comorbid obstructive sleep apnea, gastroesophageal reflux, polycystic ovary syndrome, and fatty liver disease. The surgery was performed successfully, and she tolerated the procedure well. Postoperatively, an upper GI study confirmed no anastomotic leak, and her diet was advanced from clear liquids to stage three over the hospital stay. Pain was controlled with oral Roxicet, and she remained ambulatory. She was discharged home with instructions to continue crushed medications, follow a stage three diet, avoid straws and heavy lifting, and monitor for signs of complications. Follow-up was scheduled in two weeks.
problems: Body Mass Index 40 and over, adult

EGD: Pernianastamotic Ulcerations were noted near 
gastrojejunostomy.
 
Brief Hospital Course:
The patient was admitted to the General Surgery service on 
___. CBC and electrolytes, as well as Vitals and Ins/Outs 
were all closely monitored and the approprite repletions and 
treatments were insitituted throughout her stay at the hospital. 


___: A CT scan was done which demonstrated oral contrast in 
the gastric pouch and gastric remnant suggesting fistulous 
communication between both. Up to 3.5 cm dilatation of the 
proximal efferent limb was also note, though it was stated to be 
of unclear etiology. No obstruction was noted. An EGD was done 
which demonstrated that the gastric pouch was unremarkable. The 
GJ anastomosis appeared widely patent and within 2 cm of the 
anastomosis on the jejunal side, two ulcers were noted. An 8mm 
superficial clean-based ulcer was noted proximally and a 1.5cm 
deep cratered ulcer with a flat pigmented spot at the center was 
noted distally. No active bleeding was noted. The afferent and 
efferent limbs were entered and appeared unremarkable. An H. 
Pylori serum test was also sent which was found to be negative. 
The patient's pain was controlled on IV morphine. The patient 
was started on Protonix 40 IV qDay. 

___: The patient was placed on a Bariatric 2 diet and she 
was switched from IV medications to PO Roxicet for pain control. 
She tolerated modifications to diet as well as to pain control.  


___: The patient's diet was advanced to a Bariatric stage 
III diet. The patient reports that she was having a slight 
amount of loose stools late in the evening.

___: The patient was switched to a lactose free diet to 
address the patient's diarrhea. The patient was also given 
Protonix PO instead of IV. After the patient was found to be 
tolerating oral food and medications, and the pain was well 
controlled, the patient was discharged home with appripriate 
follow-up. 
 
Medications on Admission:
- Trazadone 200mg at night
- Ursodiol 300mg
- Vitamin D
- Multivitamin
- Ca citrate
- Fe
- B12

1. omeprazole 20 mg Capsule, Delayed Release(E.C.) Sig: One (1) 
Capsule, Delayed Release(E.C.) PO BID (2 times a day): Please 
crush.
Disp:*60 Capsule, Delayed Release(E.C.)(s)* Refills:*2*
2. oxycodone-acetaminophen ___ mg/5 mL Solution Sig: ___ MLs 
PO Q4H (every 4 hours) as needed for pain.
Disp:*500 ML(s)* Refills:*0*
3. alprazolam 0.25 mg Tablet Sig: One (1) Tablet PO BID (2 times 
a day) as needed for anxiety.  

 
Discharge Disposition:
Home
 
Discharge Diagnosis:
Ulceration in the perianastamotic area of the gastrojejunal 
anastamosis.

 
Discharge Condition:
Mental Status: Clear and coherent.
Level of Consciousness: Alert and interactive.
Activity Status: Ambulatory - Independent.

 
Discharge Instructions:
You were seen in the hospital for evaluation of your epigastric 
pain three months after having a gastric bypass surgery for 
weight loss reasons. You have lost over 50 lbs in the initial 
period. A CT scan with contrast found that you have a possible 
connection between gastric remnant and the gastric pouch. An EGD 
was done that demonstrated two ulcerations on the jejunal side 
of the gastrojejunal anastamosis. A Helicobacter pylori blood 
test was ordered, which proved to be negative.

You are being discharged with instructions to take oral proton 
pump inhibitors as an outpatient that can be crushed. 

You can return to work as long as your pain is well controlled 
without narcotic medications, including oxycodone or Roxicet. A 
Doctor's note is attached. 

 

 
Followup Instructions:
___

radiology_notes.text:
INDICATION:  ___ woman with history of gastric bypass surgery,
presents with epigastric pain, now about two months after surgery.  Please
evaluate for anastomotic ulcer.

TECHNIQUE:  Contiguous MDCT images through the abdomen and pelvis were
obtained after administration of oral and intravenous contrast.

COMPARISON:  Upper GI barium study from ___.

FINDINGS:

CT OF THE ABDOMEN:  There is mild bibasilar atelectasis.  The liver is normal.
The gallbladder is normal.  There is no intra- or extra-hepatic biliary
dilatation.  The pancreas, spleen, and bilateral adrenal glands are normal. 
There is a right extrarenal pelvis.  The left ureter is slightly prominent
without evidence of obstructing stones.

No retroperitoneal or mesenteric lymphadenopathy.  There is no free air and no
free fluid.  Oral contrast is seen in both the gastric pouch and the gastric
remnant suggesting fistulous communication between both.  Oral contrast is
both visualized in the efferent as well as the afferent limb of the Roux-en-Y.
There is up to 3.5 cm dilatation of the proximal efferent limb of unclear
etiology.
The distal anastomosis site with Roux-en-Y appears normal without evidence of
obstruction or leak.

CT OF THE PELVIS:  The urinary bladder, vagina and uterus appear normal. 
There are no pelvic hernias.  There is no pelvic lymphadenopathy.  There is no
free fluid in the pelvis.

BONES:  No suspicious lytic or sclerotic bony lesions.

IMPRESSION:
1. Oral contrast is seen in both the gastric pouch and the gastric remnant
suggesting fistulous communication between both. 
2.  Upper GI Gastrografin study is recommmended for confirmation. 
3.  Up to 3.5 cm dilatation of the proximal efferent limb, of unclear
etiology. No obstruction.

diagnoses.long_title: Gastrojejunal ulcer, unspecified as acute or chronic, without mention of hemorrhage or perforation, without mention of obstruction

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Good morning. I’m Dr. Lee, one of the surgical team. You were admitted early this morning for epigastric pain. Can you tell me more about what’s been going on?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Yes, thank you. I’ve had this burning pain in my upper belly for about a day now. It’s worse after I eat. I also felt nauseous and threw up once, but it was just food—nothing strange.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: I see. Any fever, chills, or changes in your bowel movements?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: No fever. But my stools have been looser than usual—three times today, all soft and not bloody. I’m still passing gas, at least.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Okay, that’s good to hear. You had your gastric bypass surgery a few months ago and lost about 50 pounds, correct?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Yes, about three months ago. I’ve been doing well until now. No pain or issues before this.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: That helps. We’re going to run some tests to find out what’s causing this pain. We’ve already ordered blood work and a CT scan with contrast to look at your stomach and the bypass area.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Is this something serious? Could it be related to the surgery?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: It could be. One possibility is an ulcer near the connection site. We’ll know more after the CT and a scope procedure later today.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: A scope? Like an endoscopy?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, exactly. We’ll pass a small camera through your mouth to look at the stomach pouch and the connection to the small intestine. It’s called an EGD.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Okay, that makes sense. Will it hurt?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’ll be sedated, so you won’t feel much. Just some pressure. We’ll do it after the CT scan.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Hi again. Your CT scan is back. It shows contrast in both your gastric pouch and the remnant stomach, which suggests there might be a small connection between them—possibly a fistula.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: A fistula? What does that mean?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: It means there’s an abnormal passage between two areas that shouldn’t be connected. In your case, between parts of your stomach. It’s not common, but it can happen after surgery.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Could that be causing the pain and ulcers?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: It could contribute. We’re about to do the EGD to look more closely. We’ll also check for ulcers and take a blood test for H. pylori, a bacteria that can cause ulcers.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Okay, I’m ready when you are.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Hi, you’re awake. The EGD is done. We found two ulcers near the connection site—on the jejunal side, about 2 cm past the anastomosis.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Oh no. Are they bad?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: One is 8 mm and superficial, the other is 1.5 cm and deeper, with a dark spot in the center. But there’s no active bleeding, which is good.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Is that the fistula?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Not exactly. The fistula is between the pouch and remnant stomach. The ulcers are downstream, near where the stomach connects to the intestine. They may be related, though.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: What causes ulcers like this after bypass?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Several things—like acid exposure, certain medications, or even smoking. But you don’t smoke, right?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: No, never smoked.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Good. We also sent a blood test for H. pylori. It came back negative, so that’s not the cause.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: So what now?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’ll start you on a strong acid-reducing medication called Protonix, given through your IV. It helps ulcers heal. We’ll also control your pain with IV morphine for now.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Will I need another surgery?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Not right now. Most of these ulcers heal with medication and diet changes. We’ll monitor you closely.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Good morning. How’s the pain today?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Better, actually. Still some discomfort, but not as sharp. The morphine helps.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Great. We’re going to switch your pain medicine to oral Roxicet and start you on a bariatric stage 2 diet—soft foods like mashed potatoes and scrambled eggs.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Can I eat solid food again?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Not yet. We need to let the ulcers heal. You’ll stay on soft foods for now, then advance to stage 3 later.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Okay, I can do that.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Morning. Your pain is still improving, and you’ve tolerated the soft diet well. We’re going to advance you to bariatric stage 3—more solid foods, but still easy to digest.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: That’s good. But I’ve been having loose stools in the evenings. Is that normal?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: It could be from the changes in your digestion after surgery. We’ll switch you to a lactose-free diet to see if that helps. Sometimes dairy can cause diarrhea.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I didn’t think about that. I had some yogurt yesterday.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: That could be it. We’ll hold off on dairy for now. Also, we’re switching your Protonix from IV to oral. You’ll take it by mouth twice a day.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Will I need to take that forever?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: At least for a few months. We’ll reassess at your follow-up. The goal is to let the ulcers heal completely.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Good news. You’ve done really well. Pain is minimal, you’re eating well, and your labs are stable. We’re going to discharge you today.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: That’s great. What do I need to do at home?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Continue the omeprazole twice a day—crush the pill and mix it with applesauce. Take the oxycodone only if you need it for pain. And stay on the lactose-free diet for now.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: When can I go back to work?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Once your pain is controlled without narcotics. I’ll give you a note. Follow up with your surgeon in two weeks.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Thank you so much. I’m glad it wasn’t something worse.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’re welcome. You handled this really well. Call us if the pain worsens or if you notice black stools or vomiting.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I will. And I’ll keep taking my vitamins and CPAP at night.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Perfect. Those are important. Take care, and we’ll see you soon.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Thank you, Doctor.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: One more thing—avoid heavy lifting and straws. They can increase pressure on the stomach.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Got it. No straws, no heavy lifting.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Exactly. You’re all set.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I feel ready to go home now.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’re ready to discharge you. The nurse will go over your medications and paperwork.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Thank you again for explaining everything.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Of course. Take care and rest well.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I will.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’ll see you in follow-up.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Looking forward to it.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Have a safe trip home.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Thank you.

summary.summary_paragraph: The patient was admitted for evaluation of epigastric pain three months after Roux-en-Y gastric bypass surgery. She reported nausea, one episode of non-bloody vomiting, and looser stools. A CT scan revealed oral contrast in both the gastric pouch and remnant stomach, suggesting a fistulous connection, along with mild dilatation of the proximal efferent limb. An EGD confirmed two perianastomotic ulcers on the jejunal side with no active bleeding, and an H. pylori serology test was negative. She was managed with IV Protonix and pain control using IV morphine, later transitioned to oral omeprazole and Roxicet. Her diet was advanced from clear liquids to bariatric stage III, with a switch to lactose-free to address diarrhea. She tolerated oral intake and medications well, with controlled pain and stable vitals, leading to discharge home with follow-up instructions and a two-week surgical clinic appointment.
problems: Gastrojejunal ulcer, unspecified as acute or chronic, without mention of hemorrhage or perforation, without mention of obstruction
